extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Senators, legislative staff, PTO officials, patent practitioners, and patent stakeholders (inventors, companies, small businesses)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing substantive policy, procedural, and drafting criteria for S.23 (the America Invents Act) and related amendments, including priority rule changes (first-inventor-to-file), grace-period scope, USPTO funding and operations (satellite offices), and related statutory conforming edits. Focus is on how provisions affect patent quality, certainty, small inventors, and PTO efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-inventor-to-file: simplify acquisition of rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform to a first-inventor-to-file system “simplifies the process of acquiring rights,” and is described as an “essential provision [to] reduce legal costs, improve fairness and support U.S. innovators seeking to market their products and services in a global marketplace.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments in the Record emphasize that awarding the patent to the first inventor to file reduces litigation and administrative complexity. This criterion is invoked to justify priority-rule change as a means to reduce legal costs and increase fairness and predictability for businesses seeking to commercialize inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on small and independent inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: The transition “should help small and independent inventors” (as asserted by supporters) but opponents argue first-to-file would be “severely harmful to innovation, and especially burdensome on small inventors, startups, and small businesses.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations must consider whether provisions (e.g., micro-entity fee reductions, specific protections) adequately protect startups and individual inventors. The Record contains both endorsements (claims that small firms will not be disadvantaged and that the bill was drafted with attention to universities and small inventors) and objections (fear of disadvantaging cash‑constrained inventors, race-to-file costs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve patent quality and increase certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: A transition to first-inventor-to-file is described as “necessary to fulfill the promises of higher quality patents and increased certainty” that are goals of the America Invents Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy evaluation should track whether changes (priority rule, post-grant procedures, etc.) actually yield higher-quality issued patents and more predictable property rights. Supporters cite fewer disputed priority claims and feasibility of post-grant review as mechanisms to achieve this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce USPTO backlog and improve examination efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The transition is necessary to better equip the Patent and Trademark Office to work through its current backlog (noted as more than 700,000 unexamined patent applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform should be judged by its capacity to reduce pendency and backlog, lower applicant and agency costs, and make prosecution more predictable. Provisions such as encouraging earlier filings and enabling different post-grant processes are presented as contributing to efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate costly interference proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: First-inventor-to-file “eliminates costly and slow patent interferences proceedings conducted in the PTO and the courts to determine which inventor was the first to invent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One evaluative standard is whether the reform removes reliance on interference proceedings that require inquiries into conception, diligence, abandonment, suppression, and concealment—procedures characterized as time-consuming and expensive, especially harmful to small parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage early filing and early public disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The shift “encourages both large and small patent applicants to file more quickly in order to establish an early filing date. Early filing leads to early disclosure of technology to the public, enabling other parties to build on and improve the technology.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy analysis should weigh the benefits of earlier public disclosure and harmonization with provisional application practice against potential negative incentives (e.g., premature filings). The connection to treaty obligations and foreign filing behavior is also noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable post-grant opposition to improve patent quality
rubrics_metrics.description: First-inventor-to-file “makes feasible the introduction of post-grant opposition proceedings to improve the quality of patents, by reducing the issues that could be raised in a post-grant proceeding, thereby limiting costs and delay.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A criterion for reform success is whether post-grant mechanisms become practical and effective at weeding out low-quality patents without imposing undue cost and delay. The Record frames reduced priority disputes as narrowing post-grant issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect USPTO user fees and ensure agency funding for operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform should “protect the office against being a ‘profit center’ for the federal budget. That is, the USPTO fees should not be raided ... Those fees should be used to make for a quicker, more predictable patent process.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisions (or accompanying amendments) are evaluated on whether they guarantee the USPTO access to all user fees and prevent diversion of fees to unrelated programs. Letters urge voting FOR amendments guaranteeing access to all user fees paid to the agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satellite offices: purpose, selection, and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: SEC. 18 (as proposed) authorizes the Director to establish 3 or more satellite offices to (1) increase outreach, (2) enhance patent examiner retention, (3) improve recruitment of patent examiners, and (4) decrease the number of patent applications waiting for examination and improve the quality of patent examination. Required considerations include geographic diversity and an open site-selection process; a 3-year phase-in; and annual reports to Congress on rationale, progress, and whether purposes are being achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of satellite-office proposals should measure geographic diversity, recruitment/retention metrics, reduction in pendency, examiner workforce improvements, and transparency of site selection. Statutory requirements (phase-in period, reports) provide concrete accountability criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and clearly define the one-year grace period
rubrics_metrics.description: Under current law inventors have a 1-year grace period from (1) describing their invention in a printed publication; (2) making a public use; or (3) offering the invention for sale. S.23 eliminates the grace period from offering for sale or making a public use and leaves only a grace period from “disclosure.” The Record warns that “disclosure” is not defined, which will generate litigation and uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key standard is whether the bill preserves meaningful grace protections for startups and small inventors, and whether terms like “disclosure” are clearly defined to avoid litigation and chilling of investment. Stakeholder letters emphasize the grace period’s role in enabling commercialization, fundraising, and confidential development prior to filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incentivizing premature mass filings (race-to-file harms)
rubrics_metrics.description: First-to-file may incentivize inventors to “race to the Patent Office,” producing mass filing of premature applications and overfiling of ‘dead end’ inventions, which would unnecessarily burden the PTO and inventors. This is characterized as a particular hardship for independent inventors and small businesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform should be judged on whether it creates perverse incentives to file low-quality, premature applications. The Record cites Canada’s experience and warns of resource drain on small entities and added costs of outside counsel for many filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonize with international practice while accounting for substantive differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Proponents argue harmonization with first-to-file nations will make international patenting easier and less costly; opponents note many first-to-file countries allow more extensive prior art and prior user rights and often lack the U.S. 1-year grace period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper harmonization criterion assesses whether changes meaningfully align U.S. practice with international norms without unintentionally removing domestic protections (e.g., the U.S. grace period) or exposing U.S. inventors to harsher prior‑art rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain enforceability of validly-granted business-method patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation from IPO: “Vote AGAINST any amendment that would interpose substantial barriers to enforcement of validly-granted ‘business method’ patents. IPO supports business method patents that were upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court in the recent Bilski decision.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When amending patent statutes, one evaluative yardstick is whether changes unduly restrict enforcement of categories of patents (here, business-method patents) that stakeholders view as validly granted under precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conforming statutory language and board/terminology updates
rubrics_metrics.description: Drafting/conforming amendments (e.g., replace references to “Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences” with “Patent Trial and Appeal Board,” strike or rename sections, replace instances of “derivation” with “interference” where appropriate) are required to bring statutes into alignment with substantive reforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal-drafting standards require consistent terminology and cross‑reference updates throughout title 35 and related provisions. The Record provides specific enactment-level redrafting instructions and lists sections to be conformed.
